verses.zh: 那与我说话的天使又来叫醒我，好像人睡觉被唤醒一样。
verses.en: The angelic messenger[NOTE:1] who had been speaking with me then returned and woke me, as a person is wakened from sleep.
notes: See the note on the expression “angelic messenger” in 1:9.
verses.commentary:
4:1 "the angel who was speaking with me" This refers to the angel guide (cf. Zech. 1:9,19; 2:3;
4:1,4,5; 5:5,10; 6:4). These angel guides and interpreters are common in apocalyptic literature
(cf. Ezek. 8:2-3; 40:3-4; Dan. 7:16; 8:16-17; 9:22; 10:18-21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL
TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "returned" Because of the use of this same word (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal
IMPERFECT with waw) in Zech. 5:1 and 6:1, "and came again" is a better understanding
(cf. NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB). Possibly the angel had left so that the prophet could rest.

▣ "and roused me, as a man who is wakened from his sleep" The prophet was resting. However,
this was not a dream, but a vision.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

verses.zh: 他问我说：「你看见了甚么？」我说：「我看见了一个纯金的灯台，顶上有灯盏，灯台上有七盏灯，每盏有七个管子。
verses.en: He asked me, “What do you see?” I replied,[NOTE:1] “I see a menorah of pure gold with a receptacle at the top. There are seven lamps at the top, with seven[NOTE:2] pipes going to the lamps.
notes: The present translation (along with most other English versions) follows the reading of the Qere and many ancient versions, “I said,” as opposed to the MT Kethib “he said.”

The MT, supported by a Qumran manuscript, reads “seven and seven,” which would be fourteen. But Hebrew normally says “four and ten.” The LXX simply reads “seven,” suggesting the MT has a case of dittography.
verses.commentary:
4:2 "What do you see" This Hebrew word "see" (BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
is a literary marker for a new vision. It is used two times in this verse. See full note at Zech. 1:8.

▣

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta
"I said"

TEV
"he asked"

NJB, NET
"I replied"

JPSOA
"I answered"

The MT has "he said" (Kethiv, TEV) but the Masoretic scholars made the suggestion to change
it to "I said" (Qere). This type of textual confusion is common in chapters 3 and 4.

▣ "lampstand" This is the Hebrew word menorah (BDB 633), which is literally "lamp." There
are two temple precedents:

- Exod. 25:31-40, Num. 8:1-4, a lampstand in the Tabernacle which had seven branches

- 1 Kgs. 7:49, ten separate lampstands in Solomon's Temple

However, this vision, probably of the second temple, may be a different kind of lampstand. The
description does not exactly fit the menorah of the Tabernacle.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAMPSTAND

▣ "seven lamps" Each of the branches was topped with a bowl which contained seven wicks. The UBS
Text Project, p. 799, suggests the original Hebrew text had "seven and seven." It gives this reading a "B"
rating (some doubt).

▣

NASB
"seven spouts"

NKJV
"seven pipes"

NRSV
"seven lips"

TEV
"places for seven wicks"

NJB
"seven openings"

REB, LXX, Vulgate
"seven lamps"

This Hebrew word (BDB 427) can refer

- to pipes (cf. NKJV) and thereby relate to Zech. 4:12

- to the indentions on the bowl's outer rim into which wicks were laid (cf. NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB)

verses.zh: 旁边有两棵橄榄树，一棵在灯盏的右边，一棵在灯盏的左边。」
verses.en: There are also two olive trees beside it, one on the right of the receptacle and the other on the left.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The vision apparently describes two olive trees providing olive oil by pipes to a large basin atop the menorah. From this basin two pipes extend to each of the seven lamps of the menorah, for a total of fourteen pipes in all. See vv. 11-12.
verses.commentary:
4:3 "two olive trees" The lamps burned olive oil, so these are symbolically the two sources of YHWH's
abundant illumination, power, and provision (cf. Zech. 4:11-14). These same two symbols, the lamp and olive
tree, are also used in Rev. 11:3-4.

verses.zh: 我问与我说话的天使说：「主啊，这是甚么意思？」
verses.en: Then I asked the messenger who spoke with me, “What are these,[NOTE:1] sir?”
notes: Here these must refer to the lamps, since the identification of the olive trees is left to vv. 11-14.
verses.commentary:
4:4 This fifth vision returns to the pattern of one through four, where the prophet asked the
interpreting angel for an interpretation of the vision (cf. Zech. 1:9,19; 2:2; 5:6,10; 6:4).

▣ "my lord" This is the Hebrew term adonai (cf.Zech. 3:5). See note at Zech. 1:9.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

verses.zh: 与我说话的天使回答我说：「你不知道这是甚么意思么？」我说：「主啊，我不知道。」
verses.en: He replied, “Don’t you know what these are?” So I responded, “No, sir.”
verses.commentary:
4:5 The angel questions Zechariah (cf. Zech. 4:3), the point being, that without supernatural help
Zechariah (i.e., all humans) could not receive divine revelation.

verses.zh: 他对我说：「这是耶和华指示所罗巴伯的。万军之耶和华说：不是倚靠势力，不是倚靠才能，乃是倚靠我的灵方能成事。
verses.en: Therefore he told me, “This is the Lord’s message to Zerubbabel: ‘Not by strength and not by power, but by my Spirit,’[NOTE:1] says the Lord of Heaven’s Armies.
notes: It is premature to understand the Spirit here as the Holy Spirit (the third Person of the Trinity), though the OT prepares the way for that NT revelation (cf. Gen 1:2; Exod 23:3; 31:3; Num 11:17-29; Judg 3:10; 6:34; 2 Kgs 2:9, 15, 16; Ezek 2:2; 3:12; 11:1, 5).
verses.commentary:
4:6 "Zerubbabel" There is some confusion connected with Zerubbabel.

- his genealogy

- son of Shealtiel (cf. Ezra 3:2,8; 5:2; Neh. 12:1; Hag. 1:1,12,14; 2:2,23)

- son of Pedaiah (cf. 1 Chr. 3:17-19), a relative of Shealtiel

- his relationship to Sheshbazzar

- both were of the line of David (cf. Ezra 1:8)

- both were governors of Judah appointed by the Persian court

- both were involved in rebuilding the temple (cf. Ezra 5:14-16 vs. Hag. 1:14)

- they refer to the same person (see note at Zech. 4:9)

He was apparently the grandson of the exiled Davidic king, Jehoiachin (cf. 1 Chr. 3:17-19;
Ezra 3:2; Matt. 1:12; Luke 3:27). He was born and raised in exile. He becomes the symbol (cf. Hag. 2:23) of the
restored Jewish Davidic leader (cf. 2 Samuel 7), but he was never king and he was not succeeded by a
relative of David. His main task was the rebuilding of the second temple. He is usually mentioned in
connection with Joshua (relative of the exiled high priest).

▣ "Not by might nor by power" The Hebrew term "might" (BDB 298), which usually refers to human
physical strength, although it often refers to YHWH's gracious endowment of help to the needy and faithful, here
is parallel with "power" (BDB 470). Human effort, ability, and ingenuity are not capable of fulfilling YHWH's plan. Only
His power can accomplish His will but He chooses to use human instrumentality (i.e., Exod. 3:8 and 10).

▣ "but by My Spirit" This is an OT way of speaking of the very presence and power of YHWH. It was
often understood as the active force of YHWH's word and will (e.g., Gen. 1:2; Exod. 31:3-5; Num. 11:17,25,29; Jdgs. 3:10;
6:34; 2 Kgs. 2:16; Isa. 63:11,14; Neh. 9:20; Ezek. 2:2; 3:12; 11:1,5). From this developed the concept of the Spirit as
YHWH's personal agent (cf. Hag. 2:5). This was the recognition of the need for His power and presence to overcome
all of the political, spiritual, and physical barriers. Only divine action could fulfill His promises.

It is possible that since the two olive trees are discussed in Zech. 4:11-14, that here the
oil itself is being discussed. If so, then the Spirit is identified with the oil. A special anointing oil
was used to install leaders into office (priests, kings, and possibly prophets). The Spirit is the agent
of the empowering for service.

So far in Zechariah we have been introduced to several powerful spiritual personalities.

- Lord/YHWH (e.g., Zech. 1:1)

- Lord of hosts (e.g., Zech. 1:6)

- Lord/adon (e.g., Zech. 1:9)

- the angel of the Lord (e.g., Zech. 1:11)

- Satan (e.g., Zech. 3:1)

- those who were standing there (e.g., Zech. 3:4)

- My Servant the Branch (e.g., Zech. 3:8)

- My Spirit (e.g., Zech. 4:6)

Some of these are different titles for God, while others refer to angelic beings. There is an
incipient plurality in God expressed in different persons.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY, II.

verses.zh: 大山哪，你算甚么呢？在所罗巴伯面前，你必成为平地。他必搬出一块石头，安在殿顶上。人且大声欢呼说：『愿恩惠恩惠归与这殿（殿：或译石）！』」
verses.en: “What are you, you great mountain?[NOTE:1] Because of Zerubbabel you will become a level plain! And he will bring forth the temple[NOTE:2] capstone with shoutings of ‘Grace! Grace!’[NOTE:3] because of this.”
notes: In context, the great mountain here must be viewed as a metaphor for the enormous task of rebuilding the temple and establishing the messianic kingdom (cf. TEV “Obstacles as great as mountains”).
The word “temple” has been supplied in the translation to clarify the referent (cf. NLT “final stone of the Temple”).
Grace is a fitting response to the idea that it was “not by strength and not by power” but by God’s gracious Spirit that the work could be done (cf. v. 6).
verses.commentary:
4:7 "What" This Hebrew PRONOUN (BDB 566) may be "who." "O great mountain"
is imagery for obstacles: physical, personal, and spiritual (e.g., Isa. 40:4; 41:15; 45:11; 49:11) and could refer to

- the rebuilding of the second temple

- the Samaritan opposition (cf. Ezra 4)

- Jewish apathy (Haggai)

The mountain will be

- removed by YHWH's Spirit

- ground prepared for new temple (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 603)

▣ "the top stone" This DEFINITE ARTICLE with NOUN "stone" (BDB 6)
and the ADJECTIVE "top" (BDB 910) refers to

- the rebuilding of the temple (but in this context it refers to the foundation stone, not the capstone); the foundation stone had
great significance in the construction of the ANE temples

- but also may relate to Zech. 3:8-9, which links it somehow to the Messiah or the stone of Dan. 2:44-45 (i.e., the
eternal Messianic kingdom)

- the term could refer to a "headstone" from the previous temple, as a way to show (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 1027, #7)

- continuity

- holiness

SPECIAL TOPIC: CORNERSTONE,
especially I. D.

▣ "Grace, grace to it" The Hebrew term (BDB 336) is doubled for emphasis. It is also used in
Zech. 12:10 for YHWH's grace or favor. This probably refers to His blessing on the rebuilt temple (cf. Ezra 3:10-11).

This Hebrew term can also mean "beauty" (cf. NEB, TEV). JPSOA has "beautiful, beautiful!"
It is unsure if this is an affirmation related to YHWH, Himself, or about His work.

verses.zh: 耶和华的话又临到我说：
verses.en: Moreover, the Lord’s message came to me as follows:
verses.commentary: 4:8 The revelation is of YHWH, not Zechariah!

verses.zh: 「所罗巴伯的手立了这殿的根基，他的手也必完成这工，你就知道万军之耶和华差遣我到你们这里来了。
verses.en: “The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundations of this temple,[NOTE:1] and his hands will complete it. Then you will know that the Lord of Heaven’s Armies has sent me to you.
verses.commentary:
4:9 "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundations of this house" This text causes controversy
when one compares it with Ezra 5:16 and 3:6. There are several possible solutions.

- Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel are the same person.

- both princes of Judah

- both called governor

- both returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem

- both involved in laying the foundation of the second temple

- Sheshbazzar repaired and restored the sacrificial altar, but not the temple itself.

- The foundations were started by Sheshbazzar, but discontinued and restarted later by Zerubbabel.

- For a good discussion of the possibilities see Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible
Difficulties, pp. 216-219.

Also note that this is a figure of speech because Zerubbabel himself probably did not work on
the temple itself, but delegated others.

▣ "Then you will know that the Lord of hosts has sent me" Although
NASB (1971) and NKJV have the PRONOUN "me" capitalized, most other English translations,
including the 1995 Updated NASB, do not. This phrase probably relates to Zechariah (cf. Zech. 2:8,9,11;
4:9; 6:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

verses.zh: 谁藐视这日的事为小呢？这七眼乃是耶和华的眼睛，遍察全地，见所罗巴伯手拿线铊就欢喜。」
verses.en: For who dares make light of small beginnings? These seven eyes[NOTE:1] will joyfully look on the tin tablet[NOTE:2] in Zerubbabel’s hand. These are the eyes of the Lord, which constantly range across the whole earth.”
notes: Heb “these seven.” Eyes are clearly intended in the ellipsis as v. 10b shows. As in 3:9 the idea is God’s omniscience. He who knows the end from the beginning rejoices at the completion of his purposes.

This term is traditionally translated “plumb line” (so NASB, NIV84, NLT; cf. KJV, NRSV “plummet”), but it is more likely that the Hebrew בְּדִיל (bedil) is to be derived not from בָּדַל (badal), “to divide,” but from a root meaning “tin.” This finds support in the ancient Near Eastern custom of placing inscriptions on tin plates in dedicatory foundation deposits.
verses.commentary:
4:10 "For who has despised. . .small things" Some speculate that Zechariah (or other current leaders)
was taken into captivity as a young man and was now very old. He remembered Solomon's glorious temple, and
this second temple was quite modest compared to it. The differences were somewhat discouraging to the people
(cf. Ezra 3:12; Hag. 2:3).

▣ "day" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: DAY (YOM)

▣ "these seven" There is disagreement among English translations as to where this should be
placed in the text.

- as subject of "will be glad" (NASB, NKJV)

- as relating to "the eyes of the Lord" (NRSV)

They may relate to the "seven faceted stone" of Zech. 3:9 or to the seven branched and
cupped lampstand of Zech. 4:2. However, their function relates to the four angelic horsemen of the first
vision and the four chariots of the last vision.

▣

NASB, Peshitta, NRSV
"plummet"

NKJV, NIV
"plumb line"

NJB
"the chosen stone"

REB
"the stone called Separation"

JPSOA
"the stone of distinction"

NET
"the tin tablet"

The textual question is from which Semitic root does this come?

- divide ‒ בדל (BDB 95)

- tin ‒ בדיל (BDB 95)

This word combination (BDB 6, "stone" and BDB 95, #3,"tin, "plummet" occurs only here) is
uncertain (cf. 2 Kgs. 21:13; Amos 7:7-8). It was building imagery often used for destruction
(e.g., Isa. 34:11), but in this context, for rebuilding.

The plumb line or special stone had been in the
Lord's hands (i.e., exile), but now is in Zerubbabel's hands for restoration through
YHWH's Spirit, who represents His power for His purpose (cf. Zech. 4:6).

The UBS Text Project. vol. 5, pp. 400-401, gives several possible options.

- "a tin weight" (UBS gives a "B" rating, NET, see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 801, where it
is mentioned that a tin plate was often used for a message mounted on the foundation stone)

- "the stone of dividing" (NEB)

- "the chosen stone" (NJB)

- "the main stone" (i.e., cornerstone, v. 7)

▣ "eyes" This is an anthropomorphic idiom. YHWH knows all things and desires that Judah and
Jerusalem be rebuilt and prosper. However, the surrounding nations will be judged.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

▣ "range to and fro" This is the Hebrew word "range" (BDB 1001-1002, KB 1439). It is used in
several senses.

- for God's blessing, here and 2 Chr. 16:9

- for those seeking God, Amos 8:12 and possibly Dan. 12:4

- for seeking one who is godly, Jer. 5:1

YHWH's knowledge is depicted by horses (chapter 1) and chariots (chapter 6) patrolling
the whole earth (i.e., ranging throughout the whole world). Here it means that a special stone
(cf. Zech. 4:7) or a special lampstand (cf. Zech. 4:2) also symbolize His presence, purpose, and knowledge.

In a sense this imagery of rebuilding is exactly what the angel of the Lord
wanted to see from Zech. 1:12-17.

verses.zh: 我又问天使说：「这灯台左右的两棵橄榄树是甚么意思？」
verses.en: Next I asked the messenger, “What are these two olive trees on the right and the left of the menorah?”
verses.commentary:
4:11 "What are these" Again the prophet asks the angelic guide for an interpretation of the vision.

▣ "these two olive trees" From the context, both historical and biblical, they represent
Zerubbabel and Joshua, who represent the two aspects of the Messiah's person and work.

- administrative/royal (Isaiah 9)

- sacrificial/priestly (Psalm 110)

verses.zh: 我二次问他说：「这两根橄榄枝在两个流出金色油的金嘴旁边是甚么意思？」
verses.en: Before he could reply I asked again, “What are these two extensions[NOTE:1] of the olive trees, which are emptying out the golden oil through the two golden pipes?”
notes: The usual meaning of the Hebrew term שְׁבֹּלֶת (shebolet) is “ears” (as in ears of grain). Here it probably refers to the produce of the olive trees, i.e., olives. Many English versions render the term as “branches,” but cf. NAB “tufts.”
verses.commentary:
4:12 "the two olive branches" The Hebrew term, here translated "branches" (BDB 987), is literally "ear of grain"
(cf. Gen. 41:5; Isa. 17:5)." However, in this context it refers to the olive branches that contain olives from which olive oil
flows freely and continuously.

All commentators need to remind themselves that this is an apocalyptic vision. Precision,
consistency, and logic are not required! Context (literary and historical) and authorial intent are the
key interpretive elements! See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of
Biblical Prophetic and Apocalyptic.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

▣ "pipes" This word is used only here in the OT (BDB 857). It is possibly the fruit-laden
branches of the olive tree. It seems to refer to the two olive trees which supplied oil to the seven
branches by means of these golden channels or conduits.

▣ "golden pipes. . .golden oil" The same Hebrew term "gold" (BDB 262) occurs twice in
this verse. The first designated the channels through which the oil flows. The second use seems to relate
to the color of the olive oil itself, which is golden.

verses.zh: 他对我说：「你不知道这是甚么意思么？」我说：「主啊，我不知道。」
verses.en: He replied, “Don’t you know what these are?” And I said, “No, sir.”
verses.commentary:
4:13 "my lord" This is Zechariah's normal term (adonai) of address to the angelic guide
(cf. Zech. 1:9,19; 4:4,5,13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

verses.zh: 他说：「这是两个受膏者站在普天下主的旁边。」
verses.en: So he said, “These are the two anointed ones[NOTE:1] who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.”
notes: The usual word for “anointed (one),” מָשִׁיַח (mashiakh), is not used here but rather בְנֵי־הַיִּצְהָר (vene hayyitshar), literally, “sons of fresh oil.” This is to maintain consistency with the imagery of olive trees. In the immediate context these two olive trees should be identified with Joshua and Zerubbabel, the priest and the governor. Only the high priest and king were anointed for office in the OT and these two were respectively the descendants of Aaron and David.
verses.commentary:
4:14 "the two anointed ones" This Hebrew word "anointed" (BDB 844 I), which is the word for
"fresh oil," was not used for ceremonial anointing. There is another Hebrew word
used for ceremonial anointing in the OT (BDB 602), so the literal phrase "sons of fresh oil" did not
have obvious Messianic (i.e., The Anointed One) connotations. It may have the connotation here of blessed
ones or prosperity (cf. Zech. 3:10).

Context, not a lexicon or dictionary, must determine meaning. Authorial intent as expressed
in an inspired text must take precedence. A similar lexical problem with the word/concept of anointing is
found in James 5:14, where an unexpected non-religious word for anointing is used.

Joshua and Zerubbabel are both YHWH's instruments to accomplish a temporal task (rebuild
the temple) and be an eschatological symbol of the coming Messiah as a Priest-King (like Melchizedek,
cf. Genesis 14; also note Psalm 110).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: MELCHIZEDEK

▣ "the Lord of the whole earth" Zechariah has been using the term adon (BDB 10) to
address the angelic guide, but here and in Zech. 6:5 it refers to YHWH, the creator, sustainer, provider,
and lover of all creation (cf. Josh. 3:11,13; Ps. 97:5; Micah 4:13). It is exactly this universal dimension
of YHWH's character which requires Jerusalem and the temple to be restored, because Messiah will come
from the Jewish people and nation! YHWH's redemptive plan includes the Gentiles, which surely surprised
Haggai and the Jewish leadership (e.g., Zech. 9:7,10; 14:16).

SPECIAL TOPIS: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ZECHARIAH 4:1-7

1Then the angel who was speaking with me
returned and roused me, as a man who is awakened from his sleep. 2He said to me, "What do you see?" And I said, "I see,
and behold, a lampstand all of gold with its bowl on the top of it, and its seven lamps on it with seven spouts belonging to each of the
lamps which are on the top of it; 3also two olive trees by it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on its left side."
4Then I said to the angel who was speaking with me saying, "What are these, my lord?" 5So the angel who
was speaking with me answered and said to me, "Do you not know what these are?" And I said, "No, my lord." 6Then he
said to me, "This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel saying, ‘Not by might nor by power, but by
My Spirit,' says the Lord of hosts. 7'What are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel
you will become a plain; and he will bring forth the top stone with shouts of "Grace, grace to it!"'"
